The Foreign Fighter File

By: Nickolaus Bauer | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Carte Blanche brings you an exclusive interview with a South African that fled the war in Ukraine - providing firsthand proof South Africans have been sent to the frontlines by Kyiv

Unique Selling Point:
Exclusive proof of South Africans fighting for Kyiv in the Ukraine Russia war

Summary:
As South Africans who fought alongside Russian forces prepare to return home following diplomatic engagement between Pretoria and Moscow, a critical legal question surfaces:

What happens to South Africans who fought on the side of a foreign power in direct violation of the country’s laws governing military service?

Carte Blanche has secured exclusive access to a South African who enlisted in Ukraine at 19 and is now living in legal limbo as an illegal immigrant in Europe.

We call them Lerato Venter.

In the early days of the war, Lerato presented at the Ukrainian Embassy in Pretoria and was instructed to travel to Europe to join Ukraine’s military effort. As part of the effort she was sent to the Polish embassy for Schengen VISA - she jumped the queues and A travel delay — the absence of a required transit visa — postponed departure. Days later, the training facility they were initially assigned to was bombed.

Lerato ultimately reached Kyiv, where they underwent basic military training, including weapons handling. After two months, concerns grew. Repeated requests to surrender their passport and unease about the symbolic role of foreign volunteers and the potential to be used as a tragic piece of propaganda led Lerato to flee.

Now residing in Spain and seeking to regularise their immigration status as part of a recently announced , Lerato fears potential prosecution under South Africa’s Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act (1998).

Proposed scenes
Scene 1 – The context (Opening)

We run through the ongoing plight of South Africans serving in the Russian military after being duped. And how they will now supposedly return home in coming weeks after a deal was struck between Putin and Ramaphosa. But… They weren’t the only South Africans directly involved in this 4 year old conflict.

Scene 2 – The Confession (Opening)
Concealed interview. Lerato recounts leaving South Africa at 19, the embassy visit, the delayed arrival, and the bombing of the original training camp.

Scene 3 – Inside the War
Supplied footage from Kyiv: training drills, weapons handling, barracks life. Lerato describes growing doubts and the pressure to relinquish their passport.

Scene 4 – Flight and Fear
Lerato explains the decision to abscond and current life in Spain under legal uncertainty.

Scene 5 – The Law
Graphic explainer of the FMAA.
Military legal expert Rian Bode: participation or intent constitutes contravention.
Professor Michelle Nel: prosecution is legally viable but politically complex.

Scene 5 – Dirco
Dirco officials at the embassy in Madrid explain their inability to help Lerato when she presented herself. Possible doorstop of embassy staff.

Scene 6 – Diplomatic shock
Ukrainian and Polish embassy to answer allegations they sent South Africans to the frontlines.

Scene 7 – The local context
South Africans have fought for Russia, Ukraine and the Israeli Defence Forces. With Russian-aligned contractors reportedly returning home, will the state enforce the law consistently?

Scene 7 – Another South African illegal immigrant
After almost 4 years living in the shadows, Lerato will now take advantage of a fresh amnesty for immigrants illegally in Spain that will be granted a path to citizenship. We show visuals of hundreds of illegals queuing to take part in this amnesty and speak to one or two.

Scene 9 – Return to Lerato (Closing)
Back to Lerato: reflection on idealism, consequence and uncertainty.
Final question: If neutrality is policy, how is it enforced?

Why now
South Africa maintains official neutrality in the Ukraine conflict, yet its citizens have participated in multiple foreign wars. With returnees expected and geopolitical tensions ongoing, enforcement of the FMAA becomes unavoidable.

This story reframes South Africa’s involvement in this international conflict, poses questions about a domestic legal reckoning and exposes how widespread this issue could be. Carte Blanche will be the only media organisation to show a South African involved in the war on the other side of the fence.

Visual & Access
● Concealed on-camera interview
● Exclusive training footage and stills from Kyiv
● Legal graphics explaining the FMAA
● Dirco and Ukrainian embassy and Polish embassy comment requests
An exclusive, timely investigation anchored in one young South African’s decision — and the unanswered legal consequences that may follow.

2 days filming - One in Asturias and one in Madrid

Press Release:


The Foreign Fighter Files
At nineteen, she walked into an embassy in Pretoria. Days later, she was on her way to a war zone. Today, she’s firsthand proof that Ukraine has sent our citizens to the frontline. As reality set in, she fled to Spain, where she lives in legal limbo – even as South Africans who fought alongside Russian forces return home. Now, a critical question surfaces: will those who violated our laws governing military service face prosecution for fighting on the side of a foreign power?

Producer & Presenter: Nickolaus Bauer

Script:


(JESSICA VENTER)
Take my passport to be legally employed by the Ukrainian military.

(RIAAN BODE)
Our duty as South African citizens not to get involved in military assistance and foreign military affairs.

(JESSICA VENTER)
They needed expendable feet on the ground, and and they needed it fast,

(PROFESSOR MICHELLE NEL)
If you look at the geopolitics and, and where South Africa is, this is where the NPA will definitely have to make a call

(JESSICA VENTER)
I learned that I was quite handy with an AK 47.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
As the nation is gripped by the return of South Africans fighting for Russian on the frontlines against Ukraine, Carte Blanche can for the first time confirm there was at least one South African on the other side of this now 4 year old war.

(JESSICA VENTER)
I felt compelled, morally compelled, altruistically compelled to, to make a difference,

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Jessica Venter was an idealistic 19 year old online language teacher when the war broke out in 2022 as Russia invaded Ukraine. We’ve changed her name… For reasons that will become obvious.

Weeks later, she reported to the Ukrainian embassy in Pretoria,. And within days… she was on her way to the frontlines.

(JESSICA VENTER)
I had made contact with the military attache at the Ukrainian embassy and notified him of my intention to join the effort.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
So on the spot: You arrived, had an interview for how long?

(JESSICA VENTER)
For about probably ten minutes or so.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
And based on the information that you gave them, they said, come and fight for us on the front line.

(JESSICA VENTER)
Yes.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
You must understand how absolutely astonishing that does sound though?

(JESSICA VENTER)
It sounds crazy. It sounds very reckless. But in that moment, It wasn't my intention. My intention was. Was just to help.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Jessica says she was told if she could make it to Ukraine on her own, a handler would be waiting for her with a contract. She’d receive training at the Yavoriv military base near the Polish border before aiding in the war effort for a maximum period of two months. She claims she was directed to the Polish Embassy in Pretoria, where she skipped the queues and received a visa in twenty minutes.

(JESSICA VENTER)
I had 45 days, within the European Union and able to be able to transit through Poland.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
So let me get this straight. Age of 19. You rock up at the Ukrainian embassy. get marched off to the Polish embassy, and you are on a flight to Europe days later.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
And your parents?

(JESSICA VENTER)
I told my parents when I arrived at the airport in Johannesburg.

(JESSICA VENTER)
They were furious. Of course, but I think they realised very quickly that there was no, no stopping me.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Then, Jessica’s bizarre journey took a turn. Her initial flight was booked via London, and because she didn’t have a transit visa she wasn’t allowed to board at OR Tambo International Airport. That twist of fate proved vital. On the day Jessica was supposed to arrive, Yavoriv military base was bombed and up to one hundred and eighty foreign volunteers were killed.

(JESSICA VENTER)
Had I arrived two days earlier, I would have been at that base and I would have been killed in that bombing. That should have been my first sign to run.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
But Jessica persisted. After two nights on the airport floor she restarted her journey, arriving at the Polish Ukrainian border in late March 2022.
She was greeted by a long line of cars desperate to get out of Ukraine while she and a group of volunteer soldiers were on a bus going in the other direction.

(JESSICA VENTER)
I remember vividly laughing at how ridiculous it felt to sit on that bus. Me and my beanie, and a bunch of soldiers in full military gear. It looked like they were ready for combat. And here I was, pathetic, a little South African teacher,
(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Jessica claims she arrived in Lyiv amid absolute chaos and disorganization and began her training. She ended up in Kiev a few weeks later.

(JESSICA VENTER)
We didn't have bullets. We set it up with wooden weapons, wooden cut-outs shaped like AK 40 sevens.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Jessica says she became suspicious when she was constantly asked to hand over her passport, amid rumours she would be headed to the frontlines without any plan to return.

(JESSICA VENTER)
You learn the term for cannon fodder in Ukrainian within the first couple of weeks of arriving. There's a reason why you understand what Mersal means. You understand. They needed expendable feet on the ground, I do think that the Ukrainian government wanted as much propaganda as possible

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Do you think it made a difference that you were a South African?

(JESSICA VENTER)
I do think that South Africa, having this strong alliance, historical political alliance with Russia, it would have meant that a country that shares values with Russia has people within its borders who do not agree, who are willing to fight

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
After two months in Ukraine, Jessica decided to make a run for it. She boarded a train back to the Polish border, from which she made a break for Spain, hoping to take advantage of the conversational Spanish she picked up from her language teaching.

(JESSICA VENTER)
Got to the refugee centre in Warsaw and I found out that there was a bus going to Spain, and, I made my decision then and there.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
So you've been hiding out now in Spain for how long?

(JESSICA VENTER)
Three years and nine months.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
How did it feel to live? Yeah. Without papers to live illegally?

(JESSICA VENTER)
Yeah, it was horrible. It was hell. It was pure fucking hell. It's unthinkable. It really is. managed to get it back on track.I was literally sitting on the ground with my phone propped up on a couple of books, teaching English.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Jessica is now one of an estimated 500 000 undocumented immigrants who will soon be able to take advantage of a new amnesty announced by the Spanish government.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Spain has bucked the trend on immigration. Offering an open hand instead of a clenched fist. And nowhere is this more apparent than in Lavapies - the most diverse suburb of Madrid.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Rahman Muhib arrived in Spain in December soon after the amnesty was announced by Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.

(-RAHMAN MUHIB)
Lots of friends told me if I move and come to Spain and I will stay here two years, the Spanish government will give me documents. That's why I move from London to here in Spain.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
A path to legal residency and a work permit could be a way to stay out of trouble for Jessica, both here and back home. South African law is clear: Any citizen who has served in a foreign military without expressed government approval is open to prosecution.

And military attorney Riaan Bode says Jessica could be in serious trouble.

(-RIAAN BODE-ENGELSMAN INCORPORATED)
South African citizens in armed conflict upon return might be deprived or might even lose their citizenship. It could be easily defined as acting as a combatant, that’s prima facie evidence.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Which means Jessica could be stripped of her citizenship after travelling to Ukraine to fight in the war. BUT… on a balance of possibility versus probability - Military law academic Professor Michelle Nel thinks otherwise.
She suggests the issue of South Africans serving on both sides of the Russia Ukraine war could be too much of a political hot potato to take on.

(-PROFESSOR MICHELLE NEL)
it's very difficult to get the evidence that you need in court to find a person guilty you will have to get the evidence from where this incident happened. And I think one cannot shy away from the fact that sometimes political decisions are made as well, because it's got it. Well, it has the potential to have quite severe diplomatic, consequences,

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
The Ukrainian embassy confirm foreign nationals fight on Kyiv’s side with the same legal status and limited pay as Ukrainians, but say their embassies don’t recruit volunteers or have visa agreements with Poland. They add that volunteers fight for Ukraine’s survival, not for money and that Ukraine is immensely grateful to them.

The Department of International Relations and Cooperation, meanwhile, acknowledges South Africans are fighting in Ukraine, stressing that it's a criminal act to join a foreign armed force without approval. DIRCO has urged South Africans not to volunteer for armed conflict abroad.

Jessica is not planning to go back to South Africa any time soon. And chosen not to take advantage of Spain's immigration amnesty, qualifying late last year for a student visa. She also claims she was not the only South African fighting on the frontline in Ukraine.

(JESSICA VENTER)
There were a bunch of South Africans, actually, a bunch of South Africans.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
So. So, you know, for a fact you're not the only South African that went and did.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Don't you think you were being a little bit too young and stupid?

(JESSICA VENTER)
I do think so. I do think I think maybe I just had to learn what life is, the hard way.

(NICKOLAUS BAUER)
Should people feel sorry for you?

(JESSICA VENTER)
No, no, I think people should. People should feel sorry for the world and the state that it's in, and that they are impressionable young people who do stupid shit all the time.

Naivety, belief in a greater good, or just plain stupidity: Jessica’s life will never be the same.




LINK PROMO
As South African nationals returned from Russia after serving on the front line. We bring you the story of another South African from the other side. And how they fled Ukraine after two months into the war.

PROMO 1
VO:
She was 19 years old when she left South Africa… and headed straight into a foreign war.
JESSICA VENTER:
“Learning how to stuff a bullet wound and how to stop bleeding”
VO:
Now an illegal immigrant in Europe, could she lose her citizenship?
RIAAN BODE:
“They must be convinced that there is prospect of successful prosecution.”
VO:
A South African on Ukraine’s frontline.
Idealist… mercenary… or criminal?


PROMO 2
VO:
Volunteering to go to war…What was Ukraine’s plan for South Africans on the frontline?
JESSICA VENTER:
“I was quite handy with an AK-47.”
VO:
And under South African law — her citizenship could be in jeopardy.
PROFESSOR MICHELLE NEL:
“Having the intent to go and do that, they’ve already started with a punishable action.”
VO:
A war thousands of kilometres away.
And a legal reckoning waiting back home.

March 2026 - Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 15 March 2026 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Press Release: The Foreign Fighter Files At nineteen, she walked into an embassy in Pretoria. Days later, she was on her way to a war zone. Today, she’s firsthand proof that Ukraine has sent our citizens to the frontline. As reality set in, she fled to Spain, where she lives in legal limbo – even as South Africans who fought alongside Russian forces return home. Now, a critical question surfaces: will those who violated our laws governing military service face prosecution for fighting on the side of a foreign power? Producer & Presenter: Nickolaus Bauer Script: (JESSICA VENTER) Take my passport to be legally employed by the Ukrainian military. (RIAAN BODE) Our duty as South African citizens not to get involved in military assistance and foreign military affairs. (JESSICA VENTER) They needed expendable feet on the ground, and and they needed it fast, (PROFESSOR MICHELLE NEL) If you look at the geopolitics and, and where South Africa is, this is where the NPA will definitely have to make a call (JESSICA VENTER) I learned that I was quite handy with an AK 47. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) As the nation is gripped by the return of South Africans fighting for Russian on the frontlines against Ukraine, Carte Blanche can for the first time confirm there was at least one South African on the other side of this now 4 year old war. (JESSICA VENTER) I felt compelled, morally compelled, altruistically compelled to, to make a difference, (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Jessica Venter was an idealistic 19 year old online language teacher when the war broke out in 2022 as Russia invaded Ukraine. We’ve changed her name… For reasons that will become obvious. Weeks later, she reported to the Ukrainian embassy in Pretoria,. And within days… she was on her way to the frontlines. (JESSICA VENTER) I had made contact with the military attache at the Ukrainian embassy and notified him of my intention to join the effort. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) So on the spot: You arrived, had an interview for how long? (JESSICA VENTER) For about probably ten minutes or so. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) And based on the information that you gave them, they said, come and fight for us on the front line. (JESSICA VENTER) Yes. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) You must understand how absolutely astonishing that does sound though? (JESSICA VENTER) It sounds crazy. It sounds very reckless. But in that moment, It wasn't my intention. My intention was. Was just to help. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Jessica says she was told if she could make it to Ukraine on her own, a handler would be waiting for her with a contract. She’d receive training at the Yavoriv military base near the Polish border before aiding in the war effort for a maximum period of two months. She claims she was directed to the Polish Embassy in Pretoria, where she skipped the queues and received a visa in twenty minutes. (JESSICA VENTER) I had 45 days, within the European Union and able to be able to transit through Poland. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) So let me get this straight. Age of 19. You rock up at the Ukrainian embassy. get marched off to the Polish embassy, and you are on a flight to Europe days later. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) And your parents? (JESSICA VENTER) I told my parents when I arrived at the airport in Johannesburg. (JESSICA VENTER) They were furious. Of course, but I think they realised very quickly that there was no, no stopping me. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Then, Jessica’s bizarre journey took a turn. Her initial flight was booked via London, and because she didn’t have a transit visa she wasn’t allowed to board at OR Tambo International Airport. That twist of fate proved vital. On the day Jessica was supposed to arrive, Yavoriv military base was bombed and up to one hundred and eighty foreign volunteers were killed. (JESSICA VENTER) Had I arrived two days earlier, I would have been at that base and I would have been killed in that bombing. That should have been my first sign to run. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) But Jessica persisted. After two nights on the airport floor she restarted her journey, arriving at the Polish Ukrainian border in late March 2022. She was greeted by a long line of cars desperate to get out of Ukraine while she and a group of volunteer soldiers were on a bus going in the other direction. (JESSICA VENTER) I remember vividly laughing at how ridiculous it felt to sit on that bus. Me and my beanie, and a bunch of soldiers in full military gear. It looked like they were ready for combat. And here I was, pathetic, a little South African teacher, (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Jessica claims she arrived in Lyiv amid absolute chaos and disorganization and began her training. She ended up in Kiev a few weeks later. (JESSICA VENTER) We didn't have bullets. We set it up with wooden weapons, wooden cut-outs shaped like AK 40 sevens. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Jessica says she became suspicious when she was constantly asked to hand over her passport, amid rumours she would be headed to the frontlines without any plan to return. (JESSICA VENTER) You learn the term for cannon fodder in Ukrainian within the first couple of weeks of arriving. There's a reason why you understand what Mersal means. You understand. They needed expendable feet on the ground, I do think that the Ukrainian government wanted as much propaganda as possible (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Do you think it made a difference that you were a South African? (JESSICA VENTER) I do think that South Africa, having this strong alliance, historical political alliance with Russia, it would have meant that a country that shares values with Russia has people within its borders who do not agree, who are willing to fight (NICKOLAUS BAUER) After two months in Ukraine, Jessica decided to make a run for it. She boarded a train back to the Polish border, from which she made a break for Spain, hoping to take advantage of the conversational Spanish she picked up from her language teaching. (JESSICA VENTER) Got to the refugee centre in Warsaw and I found out that there was a bus going to Spain, and, I made my decision then and there. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) So you've been hiding out now in Spain for how long? (JESSICA VENTER) Three years and nine months. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) How did it feel to live? Yeah. Without papers to live illegally? (JESSICA VENTER) Yeah, it was horrible. It was hell. It was pure fucking hell. It's unthinkable. It really is. managed to get it back on track.I was literally sitting on the ground with my phone propped up on a couple of books, teaching English. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Jessica is now one of an estimated 500 000 undocumented immigrants who will soon be able to take advantage of a new amnesty announced by the Spanish government. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Spain has bucked the trend on immigration. Offering an open hand instead of a clenched fist. And nowhere is this more apparent than in Lavapies - the most diverse suburb of Madrid. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Rahman Muhib arrived in Spain in December soon after the amnesty was announced by Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez. (-RAHMAN MUHIB) Lots of friends told me if I move and come to Spain and I will stay here two years, the Spanish government will give me documents. That's why I move from London to here in Spain. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) A path to legal residency and a work permit could be a way to stay out of trouble for Jessica, both here and back home. South African law is clear: Any citizen who has served in a foreign military without expressed government approval is open to prosecution. And military attorney Riaan Bode says Jessica could be in serious trouble. (-RIAAN BODE-ENGELSMAN INCORPORATED) South African citizens in armed conflict upon return might be deprived or might even lose their citizenship. It could be easily defined as acting as a combatant, that’s prima facie evidence. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Which means Jessica could be stripped of her citizenship after travelling to Ukraine to fight in the war. BUT… on a balance of possibility versus probability - Military law academic Professor Michelle Nel thinks otherwise. She suggests the issue of South Africans serving on both sides of the Russia Ukraine war could be too much of a political hot potato to take on. (-PROFESSOR MICHELLE NEL) it's very difficult to get the evidence that you need in court to find a person guilty you will have to get the evidence from where this incident happened. And I think one cannot shy away from the fact that sometimes political decisions are made as well, because it's got it. Well, it has the potential to have quite severe diplomatic, consequences, (NICKOLAUS BAUER) The Ukrainian embassy confirm foreign nationals fight on Kyiv’s side with the same legal status and limited pay as Ukrainians, but say their embassies don’t recruit volunteers or have visa agreements with Poland. They add that volunteers fight for Ukraine’s survival, not for money and that Ukraine is immensely grateful to them. The Department of International Relations and Cooperation, meanwhile, acknowledges South Africans are fighting in Ukraine, stressing that it's a criminal act to join a foreign armed force without approval. DIRCO has urged South Africans not to volunteer for armed conflict abroad. Jessica is not planning to go back to South Africa any time soon. And chosen not to take advantage of Spain's immigration amnesty, qualifying late last year for a student visa. She also claims she was not the only South African fighting on the frontline in Ukraine. (JESSICA VENTER) There were a bunch of South Africans, actually, a bunch of South Africans. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) So. So, you know, for a fact you're not the only South African that went and did. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Don't you think you were being a little bit too young and stupid? (JESSICA VENTER) I do think so. I do think I think maybe I just had to learn what life is, the hard way. (NICKOLAUS BAUER) Should people feel sorry for you? (JESSICA VENTER) No, no, I think people should. People should feel sorry for the world and the state that it's in, and that they are impressionable young people who do stupid shit all the time. Naivety, belief in a greater good, or just plain stupidity: Jessica’s life will never be the same. LINK PROMO As South African nationals returned from Russia after serving on the front line. We bring you the story of another South African from the other side. And how they fled Ukraine after two months into the war. PROMO 1 VO: She was 19 years old when she left South Africa… and headed straight into a foreign war. JESSICA VENTER: “Learning how to stuff a bullet wound and how to stop bleeding” VO: Now an illegal immigrant in Europe, could she lose her citizenship? RIAAN BODE: “They must be convinced that there is prospect of successful prosecution.” VO: A South African on Ukraine’s frontline. Idealist… mercenary… or criminal? PROMO 2 VO: Volunteering to go to war…What was Ukraine’s plan for South Africans on the frontline? JESSICA VENTER: “I was quite handy with an AK-47.” VO: And under South African law — her citizenship could be in jeopardy. PROFESSOR MICHELLE NEL: “Having the intent to go and do that, they’ve already started with a punishable action.” VO: A war thousands of kilometres away. And a legal reckoning waiting back home.

metadata.Summary: As South Africans who fought alongside Russian forces prepare to return home following diplomatic engagement between Pretoria and Moscow, a critical legal question surfaces: What happens to South Africans who fought on the side of a foreign power in direct violation of the country’s laws governing military service? Carte Blanche has secured exclusive access to a South African who enlisted in Ukraine at 19 and is now living in legal limbo as an illegal immigrant in Europe. We call them Lerato Venter. In the early days of the war, Lerato presented at the Ukrainian Embassy in Pretoria and was instructed to travel to Europe to join Ukraine’s military effort. As part of the effort she was sent to the Polish embassy for Schengen VISA - she jumped the queues and A travel delay — the absence of a required transit visa — postponed departure. Days later, the training facility they were initially assigned to was bombed. Lerato ultimately reached Kyiv, where they underwent basic military training, including weapons handling. After two months, concerns grew. Repeated requests to surrender their passport and unease about the symbolic role of foreign volunteers and the potential to be used as a tragic piece of propaganda led Lerato to flee. Now residing in Spain and seeking to regularise their immigration status as part of a recently announced , Lerato fears potential prosecution under South Africa’s Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act (1998). Proposed scenes Scene 1 – The context (Opening) We run through the ongoing plight of South Africans serving in the Russian military after being duped. And how they will now supposedly return home in coming weeks after a deal was struck between Putin and Ramaphosa. But… They weren’t the only South Africans directly involved in this 4 year old conflict. Scene 2 – The Confession (Opening) Concealed interview. Lerato recounts leaving South Africa at 19, the embassy visit, the delayed arrival, and the bombing of the original training camp. Scene 3 – Inside the War Supplied footage from Kyiv: training drills, weapons handling, barracks life. Lerato describes growing doubts and the pressure to relinquish their passport. Scene 4 – Flight and Fear Lerato explains the decision to abscond and current life in Spain under legal uncertainty. Scene 5 – The Law Graphic explainer of the FMAA. Military legal expert Rian Bode: participation or intent constitutes contravention. Professor Michelle Nel: prosecution is legally viable but politically complex. Scene 5 – Dirco Dirco officials at the embassy in Madrid explain their inability to help Lerato when she presented herself. Possible doorstop of embassy staff. Scene 6 – Diplomatic shock Ukrainian and Polish embassy to answer allegations they sent South Africans to the frontlines. Scene 7 – The local context South Africans have fought for Russia, Ukraine and the Israeli Defence Forces. With Russian-aligned contractors reportedly returning home, will the state enforce the law consistently? Scene 7 – Another South African illegal immigrant After almost 4 years living in the shadows, Lerato will now take advantage of a fresh amnesty for immigrants illegally in Spain that will be granted a path to citizenship. We show visuals of hundreds of illegals queuing to take part in this amnesty and speak to one or two. Scene 9 – Return to Lerato (Closing) Back to Lerato: reflection on idealism, consequence and uncertainty. Final question: If neutrality is policy, how is it enforced? Why now South Africa maintains official neutrality in the Ukraine conflict, yet its citizens have participated in multiple foreign wars. With returnees expected and geopolitical tensions ongoing, enforcement of the FMAA becomes unavoidable. This story reframes South Africa’s involvement in this international conflict, poses questions about a domestic legal reckoning and exposes how widespread this issue could be. Carte Blanche will be the only media organisation to show a South African involved in the war on the other side of the fence. Visual & Access ● Concealed on-camera interview ● Exclusive training footage and stills from Kyiv ● Legal graphics explaining the FMAA ● Dirco and Ukrainian embassy and Polish embassy comment requests An exclusive, timely investigation anchored in one young South African’s decision — and the unanswered legal consequences that may follow.
